A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same language-agency research. All 17 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v2, including figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original classifier evaluations and gender, racial, and intersectional bias analyses, including statistical tests and stratified appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Mistral, Llama3, a prior agency-classifier comparison, and prompt-based mitigation experiments.

M1.justification: v2 adds an evaluated inference-time mitigation variant that appends an agency-fairness instruction to generation prompts (Section 4.4). The LAC construction process, classifier architectures, BERT selection, and fine-tuning procedures remain unchanged; much of LABE packages the existing generation-and-classification pipeline.

E1.justification: The underlying coverage remains biographies, professor reviews, and reference letters, with binary gender and four racial groups. LAC's source and the existing comparison datasets are retained. Additional LLMs and mitigation prompts operate within this coverage; reinterpreting the existing synthetic reference letters as human proxies adds no human-written dataset.

E2.justification: v2 Table 12 adds Wan et al. (2023)'s agency classifier to the LAC comparison, reporting 66.49% accuracy. v1 Table 11 already contains the retained string-matching, sentiment, BERT, RoBERTa, and Llama2 comparators. Mistral and Llama3 are additional models being audited rather than competing agency-measurement tools.

E3.justification: v2 introduces inter-group ratio-gap variance as a principal bias metric and expands evaluation to three LLMs with paired original and fairness-instructed generation conditions. New configurations include 7B/8B instruction models with a 512-new-token limit. Existing splits and preprocessing remain stable. The name-generation description changes from ten to five names per gender/race, matching the unchanged five-name lists; actual resampling is not established.

E4.justification: Section 4.4, Tables 4–5, and Appendix E add a substantial investigation of whether fairness instructions reduce, amplify, or reverse biases across models and demographic groups. The earlier KDE distribution analysis disappears. Existing profession- and department-stratified analyses are retained and relocated to Appendix E.1.

E5.justification: v2 removes the entire one-sided gender-bias t-testing protocol and six datasets' test statistics and p-values reported in v1 Appendix D.2 and Table 18. Both versions retain averaging over seeds 0, 1, and 2 and final annotation agreement of 0.90; the preliminary 0.71 agreement disappears. New cross-group variances measure demographic disparity, not uncertainty across runs.

E6.justification: Original classifier scores and ChatGPT and existing-dataset results are retained across table moves, including BERT's 91.69% accuracy. v2 adds extensive Mistral, Llama3, and mitigation results. For example, Table 4 reports overall bias changing from 56.81 to 34.02 for Llama3 and from 34.40 to 35.50 for ChatGPT under fairness instructions. These are newly reported within-v2 experimental comparisons.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.3 adds an operational mathematical definition of inter-group bias using variance of agentic–communal ratio gaps across demographic groups. v1 reports group agency levels and gaps without this variance-based definition. Neither version provides substantive theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v1 centers LAC and uncovering biases in six datasets. v2 makes the 5,400-prompt LABE benchmark a principal contribution and adds abstract/conclusion claims about Llama3's greatest overall bias, intersectional bias exceeding single-axis bias on most tasks, and mitigation causing amplification or overshooting.

C2.justification: v2 introduces amplification/overshooting interpretations, suggests models may fail to understand agency fairness, and explicitly justifies synthetic reference letters as proxies for human writing. Appendix G adds that balancing and reannotation cannot guarantee fairness. Some interpretations overreach: Section 4.2 broadly places non-White groups below White groups, although retained ChatGPT biography results place Asian agency higher.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands documentation with prompt counts, generation-model versions and settings, baseline implementation sources, model/dataset licenses, and A6000 hardware and runtime information (Section 4 and Appendices C–F). These largely document existing or newly added experiments rather than changes to retained training recipes. A LAC-release claim replaces v1's future dataset/checkpoint-release promise, but no LAC access link is supplied.

R1.justification: Most social-science and language-agency background remains. v2 adds a focused prompt-mitigation literature discussion citing Bansal et al., Ganguli et al., Huang et al., and Wan and Chang, and strengthens its criticism of Wan et al.'s classifier using the newly reported accuracy comparison.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method narrative, and results organization are extensively rewritten around LABE and four headline findings. Dataset construction receives expanded explanatory principles, appendices are reorganized, and limitations and ethics material are combined in Appendix G. Some unresolved citations and incorrect cross-references remain.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document from two columns to one, replaces the opening example table with a pipeline illustration, adds a gender-gap comparison chart, and expands the intersectional figure from three to nine panels. It also introduces summary and mitigation tables, restructures appendix tables, relocates the human stratification figure, and removes the KDE figure.

improvement.justification: The direct prior-classifier comparison strengthens validation, while additional models and paired mitigation experiments make the benchmark more informative and practically useful. These benefits are tempered by removing v1's significance tests and introducing claim–table inconsistencies: Section 4.3 calls Llama3 most biased on biographies although Table 4 gives it the lowest overall biography score, and the racial generalization exceeds Table 19's evidence. The expanded evidence supports a limited net improvement, with substantial interpretive weaknesses remaining.
